old: Built for a bigger room than this one, and kept fed accordingly. The chairs nearest it are the worst chairs in the house and they are always taken.
new: Built for a bigger room than this one, and fed like it. The chairs closest in are scorched down one side, and both of them are taken.

old: Bows, a cracked buckler, one very good spear. Nothing here was donated. Every piece was left behind by somebody who did not come back for it, and the house does not say which.
new: Bows, a cracked buckler, one very good spear. Nothing here was donated. Each piece has a name cut into it somewhere, and the house has put no card under any of them.

old: Elbow-polished to a shine along its whole length except one arm's width at the far end, which is somebody's, permanently.
new: Elbow-polished to a shine along its whole length except one arm's width at the far end, where the shine stops dead.

old: Long enough for a full company and set for four. The house leaves it that way on purpose, and everybody in the room has noticed and nobody mentions it.
new: Long enough for a full company and set for four. The factor walks its empty half twice while you stand there and adds nothing to it.

old: Names in three columns, and a fourth column with no heading. The fourth column is shorter than it was last season and nobody has rubbed it out.
new: Names in three columns, and a fourth column with no heading. The fourth is shorter than it was last season, and the chalk on it is older than the chalk anywhere else.

old: Nine pegs. Eight have hats. The third from the left is empty and has been wiped, which is not the same as being unused.
new: Nine pegs. Eight have hats. The third from the left is empty, and wiped clean where the others carry a season of dust.

old: You hang your hat on the third peg, brim out, the way the house does it. Across the room a man you have not looked at stops not looking at you.
new: You hang your hat on the third peg, brim out. Across the room a man sets his cup down and lets you see him look at you.

old: The coat is already over the chair back. You lay yours beside it, take the wrong one on the way past, and nobody in this room has raised a voice or an eye.
new: The coat is already over the chair back. You lay yours beside it, lift the wrong one on the way past, and the hearth chairs stay exactly as full as they were.

old: Two men at the far table are having a conversation you are not in. Tonight, that is all they are.
new: Two men at the far table, talking to each other. Nothing here for you tonight.

old: He inclines the hat half an inch — a genuine courtesy, not a performance of one. "A pleasure," he says, and seems to mean it.
new: He inclines the hat half an inch — a genuine courtesy, not a performance of one. "A pleasure," he says.

old: Even a couch here fits like it was fitted for you. The Brothers do nothing halfway, not even hospitality.
new: Even the couch here fits like it was fitted for you. You sleep through to morning without waking once.

old: Coppers, a dog-eared deck, and chalk tallies in three different handwritings. The game never quite ends; it just changes players.
new: Coppers, a dog-eared deck, and chalk tallies in three different handwritings. A hand reaches past you and adds a chalk stroke to the middle column.

old: Ledgers with no titles and boxes with no labels. Everything here is filed under later.
new: The ledgers have no titles and the boxes have no labels, and the third box along still carries a shipping tag with the writing inked out.

old: Army-neat. Whoever sleeps here folds corners like it still matters.
new: Army-neat. Corners squared, blanket tight, and no dent in the pillow at all.

old: Hats on pegs, every one accounted for. House rule says they stay on. Nobody explains the exceptions, and nobody asks twice.
new: Hats on pegs, every one accounted for. House rule says hats stay on, and these came off anyway.

old: A slate by the cots, chalked in two hands: addresses with no names against them, times with no dates, and a column of initials down the edge. Small work. The Brothers keep the small work moving because the small work is how they hear things.
new: A slate by the cots, chalked in two hands: addresses with no names against them, times with no dates, and a column of initials down the edge. Small work, and two of the initials repeat all the way down.

old: You take the top line off the slate and walk it across Invrisil: a package nobody described to you, to a door somebody did. Two gold, and the line is wiped before you're back through the alley.
new: You take the top line off the slate and walk it across Invrisil, no questions asked at either end. Two gold in your hand, and behind you a wet cloth is already going over the line.

old: Marker-holder's rate. The line you take is longer, the door further out, and nobody asks you to account for the way round you took getting there.
new: Marker-holder's rate. A longer line, a door further out of the way, and three gold for it instead of two.

old: The rooftops run straighter than the streets. Somebody up there knows it.
new: The rooftops run straighter than the streets. Sharp enough eyes could follow one from here.

old: Slate roofs and chimney smoke. The city keeps its second story to itself.
new: Slate roofs and chimney smoke, one ridge behind another. Picking a line through it takes sharper eyes than yours.

old: A house sign with no name on it, only a hand of cards face down and a hat on a peg. Half the silver in this city drinks here and none of it says so out loud.
new: A house sign with no name on it, only a hand of cards face down and a hat on a peg. Two men come out and let the door swing shut behind them.

old: She holds the slip at arm's length, then the shopfront number, then the slip again. Whatever address she was given, this street declines to be it.
new: She holds the slip at arm's length, then the shopfront number, then the slip again. Her slip and the door agree on the number and disagree on the name.

old: Blue-grey wool, city cut. She doesn't look at you. Nobody here looks at anybody.
new: Blue-grey wool, city cut. She has already looked past you.

old: Blue-grey wool, cut the way this city cuts it, and a walking pace she has no intention of breaking for you or anyone.
new: She is in blue-grey city wool, and her walking pace does not change when you step into her line.

old: Mustard-brown coat, good city boots, and the specific unhurried circling of a man who will not be asking anybody.
new: Mustard-brown coat, good city boots, and a third pass down the same twenty yards of colonnade.

old: A tan road-cloak with the dust still in the weave, and a Gnoll under it reading the crowd the way you would read weather coming.
new: A tan road-cloak with the dust still in the weave, and a Gnoll under it watching the crowd instead of the shopfronts.

old: You circle the block twice before it clicks: the modest COYLE AND SONS sign out front doesn't match the two wagons idling round the side, or the men counting crates like men who've been shorted before. Whatever Coyle's really running out of, the front door is the least of it.
new: You circle the block twice before it clicks. The modest COYLE AND SONS sign faces the boulevard; the two wagons idling round the side face the alley, and the men loading them count every crate twice.

old: A runner ducks out Coyle's side door with a ledger under one arm, moving with the particular haste of someone who'd rather not be noticed leaving.
new: A runner ducks out Coyle's side door with a ledger under one arm, keeps the wagons between himself and the street, and does not look up once.

old: Nothing under the colonnade but shadow. Whoever works this corner keeps night hours only.
new: Nothing under the colonnade but shadow. Come back after dark.

old: Panes racked like coins on edge. The glazier watches the street through his own stock, which is either pride or advertising.
new: A pane goes up onto the rack on edge, coin-thin, and the glazier lines his eye along it to the street.

old: Boots on pegs, sorted by wear. The pair in the window has walked to Pallass and back, if the sign is honest. Signs here mostly are.
new: Boots on pegs, sorted by wear. The pair in the window has walked to Pallass and back, if the sign is honest.

old: Ruled paper in three weights, ink in four, and a card offering a scribe by the hour in a hand that is itself the advertisement. Half the contracts argued about on this street were bought here first, quietly, by both sides.
new: Ruled paper in three weights, ink in four, and a card offering a scribe by the hour in a hand that is itself the advertisement. The door is propped open, and two voices inside are arguing about a comma.

old: Pink lacquer, gone before you turned your head. The boulevard takes a moment to remember it was doing something, and nobody on it says the name out loud.
new: Pink lacquer, gone before you turned your head. The fronts on this stretch take a moment to remember they were busy, and not one of them looks north after it.

old: The desk's own ledger reads clean — too clean, the kind of clean a man pays for. Whatever's real is hidden better than this. You'll want to know how this place is watched before you go digging further.
new: The desk's own ledger reads clean — too clean, the kind of clean a man pays for. Find out how the place is watched before you go digging for the real one.

old: [Appraise Foe] — Now you know the gap in the watch, the true ledger comes easy: tucked behind a false-backed drawer no honest desk needs. Forty gold to a 'removal man,' dated the night before Coyle's own theft: his hand, his numbers, his mistake. The drawer's second catch gives up a shallow hidden safe behind it, empty now but scored where something heavier than coin sat until recently.
new: [Appraise Foe] — Now you know the gap in the watch, the true ledger comes easy: tucked behind a false-backed drawer no honest desk needs. Forty gold to a 'removal man,' dated the night before Coyle's own theft: his hand, his numbers, his mistake.

old: The desk's own ledger reads clean, which is exactly the kind of clean a man pays for. You don't have the eye to find the real one. Not yet.
new: The ledger on the desk reads clean front to back. Finding the one it was written to cover takes an eye you don't have yet.

old: The runner ducks inside, and you finally see the whole of it: crates stacked to the rafters, more of Coyle's livery than a legitimate warehouse ever needs. Wherever the come-along ends, it ends here.
new: The runner ducks inside, and the gap in the shutters gives you the rest of it: crates stacked to the rafters, more of Coyle's livery than a legitimate warehouse ever needs. The door swings shut on the last of it.

old: The stash spot sits empty. Knowing this alley, someone will restock it.
new: The line is coiled where you dropped it. The crate it was tied to is open and bare.

old: A snag-line at ankle height, tied crate to drainpipe. Old footpad work, the kind meant to trip a running mark. Worth clearing.
new: A snag-line at ankle height, tied crate to drainpipe — old footpad work, meant to trip a running mark. Worth clearing.

old: A taut line crosses the alley at ankle height, tied off crate to drainpipe. It's clearly meant to trip someone. You can't see how to clear it safely.
new: A taut line crosses the alley at ankle height, tied off crate to drainpipe. You can't see how to clear it safely.

old: You unhook the line and coil it loose. A couple of coins sit tucked in the crate it was tied to, payment nobody came back to collect.
new: You unhook the line and coil it loose. Two coins sit in the crate it was tied to, still folded in a scrap of cloth.

old: Cleaned out — by you, earlier. The alley keeps its own inventory schedule.
new: Cleaned out — by you, earlier. Nothing behind the bottom crate now but paving.

old: A cramped apothecary corner, its burner free for anyone who knows the working. Invrisil rents everything by the hour, including this.
new: A cramped apothecary corner, the burner free and the bench rented by the hour. You would need the working to use either.

old: A severe man at a spotless corner bench, tools laid out at right angles. Everything about him says the prices are exact and the opinions are free.
new: A severe man at a spotless corner bench, tools laid out at right angles. He looks at your gear before he looks at your face.

old: Cuffs pinned back, three nibs laid out in order of nerve, and the particular stillness of a man who is paid to have heard nothing.
new: Cuffs pinned back, three nibs laid out in order of nerve, and his eyes back on the page the moment yours arrive.

old: Three weights, stacked lightest at the top, each with its price chalked on the edge of the shelf rather than the stock. Nothing here is priced where you can carry the number away.
new: Stacked lightest at the top, each price chalked on the shelf edge rather than the stock. The stock itself carries no mark at all.

old: Four inks, and the fourth is twice the price of the third for a difference you can only see in daylight. Somebody in this city has bought it every week for years.
new: Four inks in the rank, and the fourth costs twice what the third does for a difference that only shows in daylight. The man behind the counter carries a bottle to the window before he will name a price for it.

old: Worn smooth in one narrow band where a hundred people a week have leaned to sign something they had already decided to sign.
new: Worn smooth in one narrow band where the signing gets done, forearm-wide, and rough as new wood either side. A second band at the far end is much shorter and worn just as deep.

old: Nine colours of wax and one blank seal for hire. The blank is the most used thing in the shop, by a distance.
new: All nine colours on the tray have cooled hard in their slots. The tenth slot, cut for the blank seal for hire, sits empty.

old: Printed forms with the terms left open, sorted by how badly the second party will want to argue later. The thickest stack is the most reasonable-looking one.
new: Blank contracts with the terms left open, sorted by how badly the second party will want to argue later. Read the thickest stack twice.
